items.body:
Moved from discussion #3817, reported by @lukecagejessica36.

With the `gthread` worker and `max_requests`, a client reusing a keep-alive connection sometimes gets "Remote end closed connection without response".

When one thread's request reaches `max_requests`, the worker stops. Another thread may at that moment be finishing a response that announced keep-alive. When that connection is handed back, the worker closes it straight away instead of serving the request the client sends next, so the client was told the connection stays open and then loses its next request. RFC 9112 §9.6: a server that intends to close a connection should say so with `Connection: close` in the final response on it. The gevent and eventlet workers already serve that next request with `Connection: close`.

Reproduce with a WSGI app where `/a` redirects to `/b`:

```
gunicorn --workers=2 --threads=2 --max-requests=3 --max-requests-jitter=1 --worker-class=gthread example:app
```

and two clients looping on `requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/a")` (the redirect reuses the connection). One of them fails within seconds.

Gunicorn 27.0.0, Python 3.12.

items.body:
Moved from discussion #3818, reported by @zonia3000.

With the `asgi` worker, a request on a kept-alive HTTP/1.1 connection is not served until the application call for the previous request returns. Starlette and FastAPI run `BackgroundTasks` inside the application call, after the response has been sent, so the next request on the same connection waits for the background task to finish. Other connections are not affected, and neither is HTTP/2. Uvicorn starts the next request as soon as the previous response is complete.

```python
import time
from datetime import datetime
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks

app = FastAPI()

def sleep_sync():
    time.sleep(10)

@app.get("/hello")
async def hello():
    return f"{datetime.now()} - Hello"

@app.get("/start")
async def start(background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(sleep_sync)
    return f"{datetime.now()} - submitted"
```

```
gunicorn app:app --worker-class asgi
curl --parallel http://localhost:8000/start http://localhost:8000/hello
```

`curl --parallel` reuses the first connection, so `/hello` answers 10 seconds after `/start`.

Gunicorn 27.0.0, Python 3.13.

### Discussed in https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/discussions/3777
Originally posted by **tjkuson** October 21, 2026 ### Type Bug Report ### Description When an ASGI app sends `lifespan.startup.failed`, the ASGI worker does not stop gunicorn. With `--asgi-lifespan auto`, the failure is logged and gunicorn serves requests. With `--asgi-lifespan on`, the failure is logged and the worker exits with status 0, and the arbiter keeps attempting reboots that repeatedly fail. The expected behaviour is that gunicorn exits (this is my understanding of the [lifespan spec](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/lifespan.html#startup-failed-send-event) at least). For context, Starlette sends `lifespan.startup.failed` when a lifespan handler raises an exception. I encountered this issue when trying to use FastAPI with the gunicorn ASGI worker. ### Steps to Reproduce (for bugs) Save this as app.py ```python async def app(scope, receive, send): if scope["type"] == "lifespan": await receive() # lifespan.startup await send({"type": "lifespan.startup.failed", "message": "boom"}) return await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": []}) await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"served"}) ``` Run `gunicorn app:app -k asgi` and get a responsive server. Run `gunicorn app:app -k asgi --asgi-lifespan on` and the worker gets stuck in a boot loop. ### Configuration Default settings with `--asgi-lifespan` set. ### Logs / Error Output ```text $ gunicorn app:app -k asgi --log-level debug [18317] [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 18317 [18317] [DEBUG] Received lifespan.startup.failed: boom [18317] [DEBUG] ASGI lifespan not supported by app: Lifespan startup failed: boom [18317] [INFO] ASGI server listening on http://127.0.0.1:8000 [18317] [DEBUG] GET / ``` ``` $ gunicorn app:app -k asgi --asgi-lifespan on [18326] [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 18326 [18326] [ERROR] ASGI lifespan startup failed: Lifespan startup failed: boom [18326] [INFO] Worker exiting (pid: 18326) [18327] [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 18327 [18327] [ERROR] ASGI lifespan startup failed: Lifespan startup failed: boom [18327] [INFO] Worker exiting (pid: 18327) ... etc ``` ### Gunicorn Version gunicorn 26.2.0 ### Python Version Python 3.15.0 ### Worker Class asgi (beta) ### Operating System macOS 27.0.1 ### Additional Context _No response_ ### Checklist - [X] I have searched existing discussions and issues for duplicates - [X] I have checked the documentation and FAQ

items.body:
### Summary

With the `gthread` worker in 24.x–26.x, a request sent on a kept-alive connection is sometimes never dispatched to the application. The connection is then closed as idle when the keepalive timeout expires, without a response. It happens only when the application does not read the request body, and only with more than one worker. 23.0.0 is not affected.

Behind a reverse proxy this turns into 502s for POST requests (the proxy cannot retry a non-idempotent request it has already sent), or into 504s when `--keep-alive` is longer than the proxy read timeout.

### Reproduction

`app.py`:

```python
def app(environ, start_response):
    # Does not read wsgi.input, like many views that ignore the request body
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain"), ("Content-Length", "2")])
    return [b"ok"]
```

`client.py`:

```python
"""8 threads, each sends 150 POST requests over its own keep-alive connection."""
import http.client
import sys
import threading

PORT = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8000
CLIENTS, REQUESTS, TIMEOUT = 8, 150, 5
ok, stalled, errors = [], [], []


def client():
    conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", PORT, timeout=TIMEOUT)
    for _ in range(REQUESTS):
        try:
            conn.request("POST", "/", body=b'{"a": 1}', headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
            conn.getresponse().read()
            ok.append(1)
        except TimeoutError:
            stalled.append(1)
            conn.close()
            conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", PORT, timeout=TIMEOUT)
        except (ConnectionError, http.client.HTTPException, OSError) as exc:
            errors.append(type(exc).__name__)
            conn.close()
            conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", PORT, timeout=TIMEOUT)
    conn.close()


threads = [threading.Thread(target=client) for _ in range(CLIENTS)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(f"ok {len(ok)}/{CLIENTS * REQUESTS}, stalled until {TIMEOUT}s client timeout: {len(stalled)}, "
      f"other errors: {len(errors)} {sorted(set(errors))}")
```

```
gunicorn -k gthread -w 2 --threads 4 --keep-alive 75 app:app
python client.py 8000
```

### Results

Linux, Docker `python:3.11-slim-bookworm` (Python 3.11.16), `-w 2 --threads 4 --keep-alive 75`, three runs per version:

| version | requests stalled until the 5 s client timeout, of 1200 |
|---|---|
| 23.0.0 | 0, 0, 0 |
| 24.0.0 | 3, 1, 2 (plus 140–190 connection resets per run) |
| 24.1.1 | 0, 1, 1 |
| 25.3.0 | 2, 3, 3 |
| 26.2.0 | 3, 4, 0 |
| 26.2.2 (installed from the git tag, it is not on PyPI yet) | 3, 3, 6 |

- The same app reading `wsgi.input` before responding: 0 stalls on 26.2.0 and 26.2.2.
- `-w 1` with 4 or 8 threads: 0 stalls. `-w 2 --threads 8`: 3.
- With the default `--keep-alive` (2 s) on 26.2.2, every stalled request fails with `RemoteDisconnected` after 2.0–2.1 s: the connection is reaped as idle although a request is pending on it.

### Possibly related

The 26.2.1 notes fix the ASGI worker leaving "a second request sent on a kept-alive connection while the worker was finishing the first ... in the parser buffer". The gthread symptom looks the same: the request is pending, but the connection is treated as idle. In gthread, `_keepalive_after()` drains the unread body through `finish_body()` after the response is sent, so the client's next request can arrive while that drain is still reading. I have not confirmed the exact code path.

items.body:
**Environment**

- gunicorn 26.0.0 (the code path is unchanged in current master)
- CPython 3.12, `--worker-class asgi`, plain HTTP/1.x
- `gunicorn_h1c` not installed (pure-Python callback parser path)

**Symptom**

Every worker stop, both SIGTERM and the `--max-requests` autorestart, blocks for the full `graceful_timeout` and then logs `Forcing close of N connections`, where N keeps growing with worker age. It happens even when the worker is completely idle.

Production example (3 workers, `--max-requests 1000 --max-requests-jitter 500`, behind an nginx that proxies HTTP/1.0 close-per-request), captured at a zero-traffic hour:

```
06:07:18 [132970] [INFO] Worker shutting down...
06:07:18 [132970] [INFO] Waiting for 1426 connections to finish...
06:07:28 [146478] [INFO] Waiting for 347 connections to finish...
06:07:28 [134827] [INFO] Waiting for 1350 connections to finish...
06:09:13 [132970] [WARNING] Forcing close of 1426 connections     <- 115s later, same number
06:09:13 [132970] [INFO] Worker exiting (pid: 132970)
```

The counts match each worker's requests served since boot (1426 and 1350 are inside the 1000 to 1500 max-requests band; the worker logging 1426 was autorestarting for having reached it). They are not real connections: the count never moves during the whole graceful window.

**Cause**

In `gunicorn/asgi/protocol.py`:

- `connection_made()` does `self.worker.nr_conns += 1`.
- A server-initiated close goes through `_close_transport()`, which calls `transport.close()` and sets `self._closed = True`. It does not decrement.
- When asyncio then delivers `connection_lost()`, the idempotence guard returns before the decrement:

```python
def connection_lost(self, exc):
    # Guard against multiple calls (idempotent)
    if self._closed:
        return

    self._closed = True
    self.worker.nr_conns -= 1
```

So every connection the server closes first leaks one count permanently. That covers any `Connection: close` response (for example HTTP/1.0 reverse proxies), every keepalive timeout (`_keepalive_timeout()` calls `_close_transport()`), and error aborts. Client-initiated closes are balanced because `connection_lost()` runs first, which is presumably why client-driven test suites do not catch it.

`ASGIWorker._shutdown()` (`gunicorn/workers/gasgi.py`) then waits on that counter:

```python
if self.nr_conns > 0 and not self._quick_shutdown:
    graceful_timeout = self.cfg.graceful_timeout
    self.log.info("Waiting for %d connections to finish...", self.nr_conns)
    deadline = self.loop.time() + graceful_timeout
    while self.nr_conns > 0 and self.loop.time() < deadline:
        ...
```

Since the counter can never reach zero, every graceful stop runs to the deadline. Consequences: deploys that SIGTERM workers always take the full `graceful_timeout`, and each `--max-requests` recycle keeps a worker out of rotation (not accepting) for that whole window, which can starve the listen socket when several workers recycle close together.

**Minimal repro (protocol level, no sockets)**

```python
import asyncio
import logging
import types

from gunicorn.asgi.protocol import ASGIProtocol
from gunicorn.config import Config


class FakeTransport:
    def get_extra_info(self, name, default=None):
        return default  # no ssl_object: plain HTTP/1.x path

    def set_write_buffer_limits(self, high=None, low=None):
        pass

    def can_write_eof(self):
        return False

    def close(self):
        pass

    def is_closing(self):
        return True


def make_worker():
    return types.SimpleNamespace(
        cfg=Config(),
        loop=asyncio.get_running_loop(),
        nr_conns=0,
        alive=True,
        log=logging.getLogger("repro"),
        asgi=None,
    )


async def main():
    # Server closes first (Connection: close response, keepalive timeout, ...)
    worker = make_worker()
    proto = ASGIProtocol(worker)
    proto.connection_made(FakeTransport())
    proto._close_transport()      # sets _closed = True
    proto.connection_lost(None)   # guard returns early: no decrement
    print("server-initiated close, nr_conns =", worker.nr_conns)  # 1  (leak)

    # Client closes first: balanced
    worker = make_worker()
    proto = ASGIProtocol(worker)
    proto.connection_made(FakeTransport())
    proto.connection_lost(None)
    proto._close_transport()
    print("client-initiated close, nr_conns =", worker.nr_conns)  # 0


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output on 26.0.0:

```
server-initiated close, nr_conns = 1
client-initiated close, nr_conns = 0
```

**End-to-end repro**

```python
# app.py
async def app(scope, receive, send):
    if scope["type"] != "http":
        return
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": []})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})
```

```console
$ gunicorn app:app --worker-class asgi --workers 1 --bind 127.0.0.1:8123 --graceful-timeout 115 &
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s --http1.0 http://127.0.0.1:8123/ >/dev/null; done
$ kill -TERM %1
```

The worker logs `Waiting for 3 connections to finish...` with no client connected and exits only when the 115s deadline expires. With the decrement fixed (we currently carry the wrapper below in our `gunicorn.conf.py`), the same sequence exits in about 2 seconds.

**Workaround / suggested fix**

Perform the decrement wherever `_closed` flips, so each connection is decremented exactly once whichever side closes first. As a config-file workaround:

```python
from gunicorn.asgi.protocol import ASGIProtocol

_orig = ASGIProtocol._close_transport

def _close_transport(self):
    was_closed = self._closed
    _orig(self)
    if self._closed and not was_closed:
        self.worker.nr_conns -= 1

ASGIProtocol._close_transport = _close_transport
```

A proper fix could decrement in `_close_transport()` itself, or centralize the close accounting in a single helper used by both paths. Similar accounting bug fixed long ago in the gthread worker: #1387.

Happy to open a PR.

### Discussed in https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/discussions/3645
Originally posted by **rybycy** June 9, 2026 ### Type Bug Report ### Description I run gunicorn with around 80 sync workers and reload them pretty often with SIGHUP. After moving to 26.0.0 a worker died during a reload with "too many open files", which i'd never seen before. Poking at it with `lsof` / `ls /proc//fd`, the master gains open fds every time i reload and never gives them back. its epoll fds and sockets that pile up, and the master thread count climbs too (leftover `gunicorn: master` threads that just sit there). SIGHUP doesn't clear it since its the same master process, only a full restart resets it. i'd expect the fd and thread count to stay roughly flat accross reloads, not grow every time. It only happens with the control socket on. soon as i start with `--no-control-socket` the counts stay flat and the problem goes away. It scales with worker count: at 4 workers the master went from 16 to 55 fds over 5 reloads, and with 80 workers a single reload roughly quadrupled the master fds. so a small setup probably won't notice for ages, but with a lot of workers + frequent reloads it creeps toward the limit and eventually a worker can't open anything and dies. ### Steps to Reproduce (for bugs) 1. tiny wsgi app: ```python # app.py def application(environ, start_response): start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")]) return [b"ok\n"] ``` 2. start it and grab the master pid: ```bash gunicorn --workers 4 --bind unix:/tmp/g.sock app:application & MPID=$(pgrep -f 'gunicorn: master') ``` 3. reload a few times and watch the counts: ```bash for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do kill -HUP $MPID; sleep 4 echo "HUP#$i fds=$(ls /proc/$MPID/fd | wc -l) eventpoll=$(ls -l /proc/$MPID/fd | grep -c eventpoll) threads=$(ls /proc/$MPID/task | wc -l)" done ``` 4. fds / eventpoll / threads go up on every HUP. add `--no-control-socket` to the gunicorn line in step 2 and they stay flat. (on macOS the selector shows up as `KQUEUE` instead of `eventpoll`, same thing.) ### Configuration ```bash gunicorn --workers 80 --bind unix:/tmp/app.sock myapp:application ``` reloaded regularly with `kill -HUP`. the repro above uses 4 workers so its quick to run, but it leaks at any count. ### Logs / Error Output the fd count climbing across reloads (from the repro loop): ``` HUP#1 fds=28 eventpoll=3 HUP#2 fds=30 eventpoll=4 HUP#3 fds=44 eventpoll=7 HUP#4 fds=48 eventpoll=9 HUP#5 fds=55 eventpoll=10 ``` and eventually a worker just dies with "too many open files" once the master/worker fds cross the nofile limit. ### Gunicorn Version gunicorn 26.0.0 (control socket landed in 25.1.0, so i'd guess 25.1.x is affected too) ### Python Version Python 3.12.13 ### Worker Class sync (default) ### Operating System Ubuntu 24.04 (also reproduces on macOS) ### Additional Context Probable cause / fix, big grain of salt: i don't know gunicorn's internals and i haven't tried to patch it myself, this is just a guess from poking around. looks like the control socket runs an asyncio loop in a thread, and that loop isn't getting stopped when the master forks a worker, so every reload leaves another one behind holding an fd + a thread. a probable fix would be to actually stop that loop in the fork path. either way, disabling the control socket avoids it, which is what i did. probably related: discussions #3528 / #3509 are about the control socket *deadlocking* workers on fork. different symptom (mine leaks, doesn't hang) but same feature, might share a root cause. i think i might be hitting that deadlock separately too. ### Checklist - [X] I have searched existing discussions and issues for duplicates - [X] I have checked the documentation and FAQ
items.title: Control socket leaks fds + threads on every SIGHUP reload until a worker hits "too many open files"

## Summary
`gunicorn/http/wsgi.py:140-167` — the `wsgi.early_hints` callback constructs 103 Early Hints responses with zero header validation, while the main response path (`process_headers`) validates against `TOKEN_RE` and `HEADER_VALUE_RE`.

A WSGI app passing unsanitized data to early_hints could enable HTTP response splitting via CRLF injection.

## Suggested Fix
Apply the same `TOKEN_RE`/`HEADER_VALUE_RE` validation used in `process_headers` to the early_hints callback.

items.body:
## Summary

Add a `--max-worker-memory` configuration option that gracefully restarts workers when their resident set size (RSS) exceeds a configurable threshold in MB.

## Motivation

While `--max-requests` helps limit damage from memory leaks by recycling workers after a fixed number of requests, it cannot catch cases where a single request (or a small number of requests) causes disproportionate memory growth. A memory-based limit provides a direct safety net regardless of request patterns.

This has been discussed previously in #124 and #1299.

## Implementation

PR #3580 implements this feature:

- New `MaxWorkerMemory` config setting (int, default `0` = disabled, units: MB)
- `_get_rss()` reads `/proc/self/status` VmRSS on Linux, falls back to `resource.getrusage` on other platforms (stdlib only, no new dependencies)
- Memory check wired into all worker types (sync, gthread, gevent, eventlet, tornado, ASGI)
- Check is skipped entirely when the feature is disabled (zero overhead for existing deployments)

## Usage

```console
$ gunicorn app:app --max-worker-memory 512 --workers 4
```

Workers exceeding 512 MB RSS will be gracefully restarted after completing their current request.
items.title: Add --max-worker-memory option to recycle workers by RSS usage

items.body:
### Summary
After upgrading to Gunicorn 25.1.0, we started seeing intermittent hard hangs during worker startup.

The master process remains alive, but a worker can block indefinitely while logging its boot message.

### Environment
- Gunicorn: 25.1.0
- Python: 3.11
- Worker class: uvicorn worker (`uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker`)
- OS: Linux containers

### Airflow context
This occurs in Apache Airflow API server mode (`airflow api-server`) when configured to use Gunicorn.

Relevant behavior in this path:
- `preload_app=True`
- master/worker forking model
- startup logging immediately after fork

Integration path in Airflow:
- https://github.com/apache/airflow/pull/60940

### Observed behavior
When a hang happens:
- master main thread is idle in `wait_for_signals`
- a background control-socket loop thread is present in master (`Thread-1 (_run_loop)`)
- worker is blocked in logging path (`logging.StreamHandler.emit` -> lock acquisition / `PyThread_acquire_lock_timed`)
- last attempted log line is typically `Booting worker with pid: ...`

The process does not crash; it stalls indefinitely.

### Representative py-spy excerpt from a hung run

<details>
<summary>Master process thread stack (idle main thread)</summary>

```text
Thread 7 (idle): "MainThread"
    0x7fc6d83a2f16 (libc.so.6)
    0x7fc6d83ad116 (libc.so.6)
    PyThread_acquire_lock_timed (libpython3.11.so.1.0)
    0x7fc6d7a1b548 (_queue.cpython-311-x86_64-linux-gnu.so)
    0x7fc6d7a1b74b (_queue.cpython-311-x86_64-linux-gnu.so)
    wait_for_signals (gunicorn/arbiter.py:394)
        Arguments:
            self: <AirflowArbiter at 0x7fc6ce7151d0>
            timeout: 1
        Locals:
            signals: []
    run (gunicorn/arbiter.py:229)
        Arguments:
            self: <AirflowArbiter at 0x7fc6ce7151d0>
    run (airflow/api_fastapi/gunicorn_app.py:189)
        Arguments:
            self: <AirflowGunicornApp at 0x7fc6d77c6090>
    _run_api_server_with_gunicorn (airflow/cli/commands/api_server_command.py:98)
        Arguments:
            args: <Namespace at 0x7fc6cde42350>
            apps: "all"
            num_workers: 1
            worker_timeout: 120
            proxy_headers: False
        Locals:
            create_gunicorn_app: <function at 0x7fc6cdd651c0>
            ssl_cert: None
            ssl_key: None
            log_level: "info"
            access_log_enabled: True
            gunicorn_app: <AirflowGunicornApp at 0x7fc6d77c6090>
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>First/only worker stack (blocked while logging boot message)</summary>

```text
Process 12: gunicorn: worker [gunicorn]
Python v3.11.14 (/usr/local/bin/python3.11)
Parent Process 7: gunicorn: master [gunicorn]

Thread 12 (idle): "MainThread"
    0x7fc6d83a2f16 (libc.so.6)
    0x7fc6d83add90 (libc.so.6)
    PyThread_acquire_lock_timed (libpython3.11.so.1.0)
    emit (logging/__init__.py:1113)
        Arguments:
            self: <StreamHandler at 0x7fc6cdeef850>
            record: <LogRecord at 0x7fc6d43f7050>
        Locals:
            msg: "[2026-02-25 21:04:21 +0000] [12] [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 12"
            stream: <_io.TextIOWrapper at 0x7fc6d81d8040>
```

</details>

### Expected behavior
Worker should boot successfully or fail explicitly, but should not deadlock.

### Workarounds that consistently avoid the hang
1. Pin Gunicorn to `<25.1.0`
2. Keep 25.1.0 but disable control socket (`--no-control-socket`)

### Why this seems 25.1.0-specific
The issue appears after moving to 25.1.0 and disappears with either workaround above.

### Minimal config shape
```bash
gunicorn \
  --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker \
  --preload \
  --workers 1 \
  <app>
```

(And it stops hanging in our environment when adding `--no-control-socket`.)

### Ask
Is this a known issue/regression in 25.1.0? Happy to provide additional sanitized traces and test any candidate fix.

There's a significant behavioral change in the gthread worker between v23 and v24+/v25: v23 behavior (gunicorn/workers/gthread.py): ``` def accept(self, server, listener): sock, client = listener.accept() conn = TConn(self.cfg, sock, client, server) self.nr_conns += 1 # Register with poller - wait for data to be ready with self._lock: self.poller.register(conn.sock, selectors.EVENT_READ, partial(self.on_client_socket_readable, conn)) ``` Connections are registered with the selector first. Only when data is available (socket readable) does the connection get submitted to the thread pool. Thread slots are only used when there's actual work to do. v25 behavior: ``` def accept(self, listener): client_sock, client_addr = listener.accept() self.nr_conns += 1 conn = TConn(self.cfg, client_sock, client_addr, listener.getsockname()) # Submit directly to thread pool self.enqueue_req(conn) ``` Connections are immediately submitted to the thread pool after accept(). Threads then block waiting for HTTP request data to arrive. With workers=1 and threads=4: - v23: 4 threads process actual requests efficiently - v25: 4 threads can get blocked waiting for data from slow clients or network latency... So, most probably If the thread pool is saturated (all 4 threads waiting for data or processing requests), the health check request cannot be serviced, causing the 30-second timeout. This need to be fixed. ### Discussed in https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/discussions/3516
Originally posted by **BehnazMoradabadi** February 18, 2026 ### Type Bug Report ### Description We had a container based on Django + Gunicorn 23 with these readinessProb and strartupProb and it was working fine: ``` startupProbe: failureThreshold: 3 httpGet: path: /health/liveness/ port: 8080 scheme: HTTP initialDelaySeconds: 30 periodSeconds: 10 successThreshold: 1 timeoutSeconds: 10 readinessProbe: exec: command: - wget - -O - /dev/null - http://localhost:8080/health/readiness/ failureThreshold: 3 initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 10 successThreshold: 1 timeoutSeconds: 30 ``` after upgrading to gunicorn 25, k8s starts considering the pod unhealthy with ``` Warning Unhealthy 16s kubelet Readiness probe failed: command timed out: "wget -O /dev/null http://localhost:8080/health/readiness/" timed out after 30s ``` Rediness function does nothing except sending an empty response: ``` def readiness(self, request): return HttpResponse() ``` I don't see any weird log in the pod. It seems to be working, but it gets restarted constantly. Can you please help me how to debug this furthur. No spike in the cpu or memory or even data transfer ### Steps to Reproduce (for bugs) _No response_ ### Configuration ```bash bind = "[::]:8080" access_log_format = '%(h)s - %(u)s [%(t)s] "%(r)s" %(s)s %(b)s "%(f)s" "%(a)s"' accesslog = "-" disable_redirect_access_to_syslog = True errorlog = "-" graceful_timeout = 60 workers = 1 threads = 4 timeout = 60 ``` ### Logs / Error Output ```text Warning Unhealthy 16s kubelet Readiness probe failed: command timed out: "wget -O /dev/null http://localhost:8080/health/readiness/" timed out after 30s ``` ### Gunicorn Version gunicorn 25.0.3 ### Python Version python:3.12 ### Worker Class sync (default) ### Operating System alpine3.19 ### Additional Context _No response_ ### Checklist - [X] I have searched existing discussions and issues for duplicates - [X] I have checked the documentation and FAQ

items.body:
## Description

When using the ASGI worker with async database libraries (SQLAlchemy async, asyncmy, etc.), client disconnections cause `CancelledError` to propagate through database operations, breaking connection pool cleanup.

Reported in: #3479

## Root Cause

In `gunicorn/asgi/protocol.py`, when a client disconnects, `connection_lost()` immediately cancels the request task:

```python
def connection_lost(self, exc):
    ...
    if self._task and not self._task.done():
        self._task.cancel()  # Immediate cancellation
```

This aggressive cancellation propagates `CancelledError` through the app, including to async database operations. When SQLAlchemy's connection pool tries to clean up (rollback), it fails because the underlying async stream is also cancelled.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a FastAPI app with async SQLAlchemy and MySQL (asyncmy driver)
2. Run with gunicorn ASGI worker
3. Send rapid requests and disconnect before they complete
4. Observe `CancelledError` exceptions in the logs

Reproduction repo: https://github.com/vpmedia/gunicorn-asgi-testing

## Error Output

```
ERROR:sqlalchemy.pool.impl.AsyncAdaptedQueuePool:Exception during reset or similar
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "asyncmy/connection.pyx", line 670, in _read_bytes
  File ".../asyncio/streams.py", line 769, in readexactly
    await self._wait_for_data('readexactly')
  File ".../asyncio/streams.py", line 539, in _wait_for_data
    await self._waiter
asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError
```

## Expected Behavior

The ASGI worker should handle client disconnects gracefully, allowing the application to clean up resources (like database connections) before task cancellation.

## Environment

- gunicorn 25.0.1
- Python 3.13
- Worker: asgi
- SQLAlchemy 2.x with asyncmy driver
items.title: ASGI worker: CancelledError propagates to async database operations on client disconnect

### Discussed in https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/discussions/3481
Originally posted by **markjm** February 2, 2026 Thanks for maintaining that great project! Below is my first bug report here so please let me know if anything is unclear! ### Type Bug Report ### Description It seems that v25 has changed some import ordering which can break gevent-patch-using projects. Specifically, `concurrent.futures` now seems to be imported before any use-defined code runs. This is relevant for gevent-based projects, because `concurrent.futures` holds references to certain `threading` threads, which can not be patched after import time. In our project, we have identified that this missed patching causes issues with other packages which use `concurrent.futures`. Specifically `boto3` s3 operations can start hanging. We fortunately have a hard startup fail to catch this otherwise-difficult-to-notice patching issue, which is why we caught this ```python for module in ["concurent.futures"]: if module in sys.modules: raise RuntimeError( f"'{module}' was detected before gevent patch. gevent patch must be imported before any other modules that use {module}" ) ``` ### Steps to Reproduce (for bugs) I have created a single-file repro with steps in: https://gist.github.com/markjm/9f724364619c519892e8111fe6520ca6 This demonstrated that some non-patched threads linger in concurrent.futures. I am not 100% sure that the example one i used (`_global_shutdown_lock`) is the one which causes issues at runtime, but i think it demonstrated the problem ### Configuration ```bash gunicorn echo:app -c echo.py ``` ### Logs / Error Output ```text v24 output: === LOCK COMPARISON TABLE === Check | BEFORE PATCH | AFTER PATCH ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Type | | Module | gevent.thread | gevent.thread Is GeventLockType? | True | True Is _thread.LockType? | True | True ``` v25 output: ``` === LOCK COMPARISON TABLE === Check | BEFORE PATCH | AFTER PATCH ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Type | | Module | _thread | gevent.thread Is GeventLockType? | False | True Is _thread.LockType? | False | True ``` ### Gunicorn Version gunicorn (version 25.0.0) ### Python Version Python 3.12.10 ### Worker Class gevent ### Operating System Ubuntu 24.04 ### Additional Context _No response_ ### Checklist - [X] I have searched existing discussions and issues for duplicates - [X] I have checked the documentation and FAQ

It looke li’e the way we finish to read the body in gthread worker has issue with ssl requests. Last update introduced signofcant changes in this worker. I.m looking at it. ### Discussed in https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/discussions/3447
Originally posted by **NZHYDROGEN** January 23, 2026 ### Type Bug Report ### Description Environment - Gunicorn: 24.0.0 (issue), 23.0.0 (no issue) - Python: 3.13.11 (in Docker python:3.13-slim) - Framework: Flask + werkzeug - TLS: gunicorn terminating TLS via --certfile/--keyfile - OS: Linux (Docker) - Requests clients: python-requests 2.32.5 (peer and load tool) Observed behavior After upgrading to gunicorn 24.0.0, we started seeing frequent errors when parsing JSON request bodies across multiple endpoints (tx, health, toh). The error appears during request.get_json() and the stack trace shows: ssl.SSLWantReadError: The operation did not complete (read) (_ssl.c:26xx) Gunicorn logs “Invalid request…” with the same SSLWantReadError. This happens on internal node‑to‑node requests and external clients. Expected behavior Requests should be read fully; request.get_json() should not fail under normal load. This did not occur with gunicorn 23.0.0. Workaround Pinning gunicorn to 23.0.0 eliminates the issue entirely. ### Steps to Reproduce (for bugs) 1. Run Flask app on gunicorn 24.0.0 with TLS enabled. 2. Send POST JSON requests (small 255–450 byte bodies) from python-requests clients. 3. Intermittently, server fails in request.get_json() with SSLWantReadError. 4. Downgrade to gunicorn 23.0.0 → issue disappears. ### Configuration ```bash Environment - Gunicorn: 24.0.0 (issue), 23.0.0 (no issue) - Python: 3.13.11 (in Docker python:3.13-slim) - Framework: Flask + werkzeug - TLS: gunicorn terminating TLS via --certfile/--keyfile - OS: Linux (Docker) - Requests clients: python-requests 2.32.5 (peer and load tool) Observed behavior After upgrading to gunicorn 24.0.0, we started seeing frequent errors when parsing JSON request bodies across multiple endpoints (tx, health, toh). The error appears during request.get_json() and the stack trace shows: ssl.SSLWantReadError: The operation did not complete (read) (_ssl.c:26xx) Gunicorn logs “Invalid request…” with the same SSLWantReadError. This happens on internal node‑to‑node requests and external clients. Expected behavior Requests should be read fully; request.get_json() should not fail under normal load. This did not occur with gunicorn 23.0.0. Workaround Pinning gunicorn to 23.0.0 eliminates the issue entirely. ``` ### Logs / Error Output ```text ssl.SSLWantReadError: The operation did not complete (read) (_ssl.c:2648 ``` ### Gunicorn Version gunicorn 24.0.0 ### Python Version python 3.13.11 ### Worker Class sync (default) ### Operating System ubuntu ### Additional Context _No response_ ### Checklist - [X] I have searched existing discussions and issues for duplicates - [X] I have checked the documentation and FAQ

items.body:
(note - I'm not asking for someone to create a solution on this. I want to gauge if a proposed solution would be acceptable as a PR that I would create)

I've run into a situation where my worker startup takes a fairly long time, and I need to increase the worker timeout to cover that. But once the worker is up, that timeout is far too long to catch a problem, especially with gevent workers (where the timeout is not tied to request times). For example, my workers take 2-3 minutes to start up normally (with some outliers), but I really only want to have the timeout at 3-5 seconds so a worker failure is detected and handled quickly enough to not cause serious impact.

For a variety of reasons (complex code base, preload is not a working solution for us, not being able to get down to sub 10 seconds even at that) shortening worker startup isn't an option. What I would like to have is a configurable grace period for the timeout. So if I set the grace period to 5 minutes, this would be what happens:

1. arbiter starts a new worker. The time of the start is tracked
2. worker starts up - this will take 2 minutes to complete before the timeout loop is active
3. arbiter checks for the worker checking in, which it is not. Since the time is currently earlier than `start time + grace period`, it ignores it
4. Repeat step 3 for 2 minutes
5. worker completes startup and starts the timeout checkin loop
6. arbiter checks for the worker checking in, which it sees at `start time + 2 minutes`. It clears the grace period
7. arbiter now expects to see the worker check in at least every `timeout` seconds, or it will reap the worker.

If for some reason the worker did not start properly and did not get to the timeout checkin loop, the arbiter would see this at "start time + grace period" and follow the normal process for reaping the worker and restarting it. If the worker.

If I've missed a way to do this already, I'd appreciate a pointer. Otherwise, if this sounds like a reasonable approach I am happy to create a PR for it for further review and refining.
items.title: Worker timeout needs to be set too long to account for worker startup
